title: When the article disappears: definiteness exceptions
title_target: Livet är för kort för dåligt kaffe.
goal: Learn the words that switch off Swedish double definiteness — *nästa, förra, samma, denna, hela, själva*, possessives — and when a noun used in general takes the definite form, the indefinite form, or nothing at all.
bekal: you can say *nästa vecka* but *förra veckan*, *min läkare* but *hela dagen*, without hesitating
you can switch between spoken *den här veckan* and written *denna vecka*
you can talk in general terms the Swedish way: *Livet är kort*, *Kaffe är dyrt*, *Hon är läkare*, *Har du bil?*
wave: Go back to Svenska 102, Unit 9: read the table with *den här / det där* + definite noun and *min nya cykel* aloud, then say each phrase again in this unit's formal style: *den här cykeln* → *denna cykel*, *det där huset* → *detta hus*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ett samtal till vårdcentralen
dialogs.intro: Dian has had a sore throat for days, and this morning the fever came back. She calls her health center in Majorna before work — or rather, instead of work.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Vårdcentralen, du pratar med sjuksköterskan Eva.
lines.id: Health center, you're speaking to Eva, the nurse.
lines.literal: health-center-the, you talk with nurse-the Eva.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Hej! Jag har haft ont i halsen hela veckan, och nu har jag feber igen.
lines.id: Hi! I've had a sore throat all week, and now I've got a fever again.
lines.literal: hi! I have had pain in throat-the whole week-the, and now have I fever again.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Igen? Har du varit sjuk tidigare i höst?
lines.id: Again? Have you been ill earlier this fall?
lines.literal: again? have you been sick earlier in autumn?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, förra månaden. Det var samma symtom då.
lines.id: Yes, last month. It was the same symptoms then.
lines.literal: yes, last month-the. it was same symptoms then.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Har du träffat någon läkare här förut?
lines.id: Have you seen a doctor here before?
lines.literal: have you met any doctor here before?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, förra gången träffade jag doktor Berg. Hon var jättebra.
lines.id: Yes, last time I saw Dr. Berg. She was great.
lines.literal: yes, last time-the met I doctor Berg. she was giant-good.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Doktor Bergs mottagning är tyvärr full hela veckan. Men det finns en tid nästa måndag.
lines.id: Unfortunately Dr. Berg's appointments are full all week. But there's a slot next Monday.
lines.literal: doctor Berg's reception is unfortunately full whole week-the. but it exists a time next Monday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nästa måndag? Finns det ingen tid tidigare?
lines.id: Next Monday? Isn't there anything earlier?
lines.literal: next Monday? exists it no time earlier?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Om det är bråttom kan du träffa en annan läkare samma dag — idag klockan fyra.
lines.id: If it's urgent, you can see another doctor the same day — today at four.
lines.literal: if it is hurry can you meet an other doctor same day — today clock-the four.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Perfekt, då tar jag den tiden.
lines.id: Perfect, then I'll take that slot.
lines.literal: perfect, then take I that time-the.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Bra. Ta med din legitimation, och gå inte till jobbet med feber.
lines.id: Good. Bring your ID, and don't go to work with a fever.
lines.literal: good. take with your identification, and go not to job-the with fever.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej då, jag stannar hemma. Själva halsen är inte så farlig, men jag är så trött.
lines.id: No, no, I'll stay home. The throat itself isn't so bad, but I'm so tired.
lines.literal: no then, I stay at-home. self-the throat-the is not so dangerous, but I am so tired.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Det låter som en vanlig förkylning, men läkaren tittar på det. Krya på dig!
lines.id: It sounds like an ordinary cold, but the doctor will take a look. Get well soon!
lines.literal: it sounds like an ordinary cold, but doctor-the looks on it. recover on you!

notes: **Hela veckan** — *hela* (whole, all) takes the definite noun but no *den* in front: *hela veckan, hela dagen, hela tiden* (all the time). Never *den hela veckan*. *Halva* works the same way: *halva dagen*. With names of places there is no ending to add: *hela Sverige, hela Göteborg*.

**Förra månaden** / **förra gången** vs **nästa måndag** — the two most confusing neighbors in Swedish. *Förra* (last) takes the **definite** noun: *förra veckan, förra året, förra gången*. *Nästa* (next) takes the **indefinite** noun: *nästa vecka, nästa år, nästa gång*. Neither ever takes *den*. Learn them as fixed pairs.

**Samma symtom** / **samma dag** — *samma* (same) is followed by the **indefinite** noun and no article at all: *samma dag, samma sak, samma problem*. English needs "the same day"; Swedish just says "same day". A *symtom* (**süm-TOHM**) is a symptom; the plural is the same word.

**Doktor Bergs mottagning** / **din legitimation** — after any possessive, the noun stays indefinite: *min läkare, Karins kontor, doktor Bergs mottagning*. You learned this rule for *min cykel* back in Svenska 101; it holds for every possessive, including the *-s* genitive. *En mottagning* (**MOT-tahg-ning**) is a reception or a doctor's practice; *en legitimation* (**leh-gi-ti-mah-HWOON**) — *leg* in speech — is a photo ID.

**Den tiden** vs **själva halsen** — *den* + definite noun is ordinary double definiteness ("that slot"). But *själva* (**HWEL-vah**, "the … itself") swallows the *den*: *själva halsen* = the throat itself, *själva idén* = the idea itself. The fixed phrase *i själva verket* means "in fact, actually".

**Krya på dig!** (**KRÜ-ah poh day**) — "Get well soon!", from the old verb *krya på sig* (to recover). Swedes say it to anyone who is ill, including colleagues, in emails and text messages. The plural is *Krya på er!*

grammars.title: Words that cancel the article
body: Normally an adjective in front of a definite noun brings *den/det/de* with it: *den långa veckan*. But a group of common words breaks this rule. Some take the definite noun without *den*; others take the indefinite noun.

head: Word
Noun form
Example
rows: nästa vecka, samma dag, följande år
denna vecka, detta kaffe, dessa regler

after: **Den här / det här / de här** (spoken) take the definite noun: *den här veckan*. **Denna / detta / dessa** (written and formal) take the indefinite: *denna vecka*. Both mean "this/these". In parts of Sweden people also say *denna veckan* in speech, but in writing stick to *denna vecka*.
An adjective after a possessive or *denna* still takes its definite ending, even though the noun doesn't: *min nya cykel*, *denna långa vecka*, *nästa stora projekt*.
With an adjective, *hela* and *halva* take *den* back: *hela den långa veckan*, *halva den gamla staden*. Only the bare *hela veckan* drops it.
*Första* and *sista* with time words usually drop *den* too: *första gången, sista dagen*. With *den* (*den sista dagen*) it is also correct, just a little more emphatic.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kaffe eller kaffet?
dialogs.intro: A week later Dian is back at the office at Lindholmen, still a little pale. At the Thursday fika, Mattias and Leila try to cure her — with coffee and a grammar lesson.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Välkommen tillbaka, Dian! Hur mår du?
lines.id: Welcome back, Dian! How are you feeling?
lines.literal: welcome back, Dian! how feel you?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Mycket bättre, tack. Jag låg i sängen nästan hela förra veckan.
lines.id: Much better, thanks. I was in bed almost all of last week.
lines.literal: much better, thanks. I lay in bed-the almost whole last week-the.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Stackars dig. Här, ta en kopp kaffe. Kaffe hjälper mot allt.
lines.id: You poor thing. Here, have a cup of coffee. Coffee helps with everything.
lines.literal: poor you. here, take a cup coffee. coffee helps against everything.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Gör det verkligen det? Läkaren sa att jag skulle dricka te.
lines.id: Does it really? The doctor said I should drink tea.
lines.literal: does it really that? doctor-the said that I should drink tea.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Läkare vet ingenting om kaffe. Livet är för kort för dåligt kaffe.
lines.id: Doctors know nothing about coffee. Life is too short for bad coffee.
lines.literal: doctors know nothing about coffee. life-the is too short for bad coffee.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vänta — varför säger man ”livet” men ”kaffe”, utan -t?
lines.id: Wait — why do you say "livet" but "kaffe", without the -t?
lines.literal: wait — why says one life-the but coffee, without -t?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Bra fråga. Abstrakta saker som livet, döden och kärleken får ofta bestämd form.
lines.id: Good question. Abstract things like life, death and love often take the definite form.
lines.literal: good question. abstract things like life-the, death-the and love-the get often definite form.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Men ämnen som kaffe, mjölk och vatten står utan artikel när man pratar allmänt.
lines.id: But substances like coffee, milk and water have no article when you talk in general.
lines.literal: but substances like coffee, milk and water stand without article when one talks generally.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och när säger man ”kaffet”, då?
lines.id: And when do you say "kaffet", then?
lines.literal: and when says one coffee-the, then?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: När man menar ett visst kaffe — till exempel det här kaffet, som Mattias har gjort.
lines.id: When you mean a particular coffee — for example this coffee here, which Mattias made.
lines.literal: when one means a certain coffee — for example the here coffee-the, which Mattias has made.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Och detta kaffe är Göteborgs bästa, om jag får säga det själv.
lines.id: And this coffee is the best in Göteborg, if I may say so myself.
lines.literal: and this coffee is Göteborg's best, if I may say it self.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Båda sakerna stämmer nog. Men jag håller mig till teet den här veckan.
lines.id: Both things are probably true. But I'm sticking to tea this week.
lines.literal: both things-the tally probably. but I hold myself to tea-the the here week-the.

notes: **I sängen** — where English says "in bed" with no article, Swedish uses the definite form: *ligga i sängen*. The same goes for many everyday places: *på jobbet* (at work), *i skolan* (at school), *på sjukhuset* (in the hospital), *i stan* (in town). Learn them as fixed phrases.

**Kaffe hjälper mot allt** — a mass noun (something you can't count: coffee, milk, water, money) used in general takes **no article at all**: *Kaffe är gott*, *Vatten är viktigt*. English does the same here. Notice *mot* (against) after *hjälpa* for remedies: *Det här hjälper mot huvudvärk.*

**Läkare vet ingenting om kaffe** — a plural noun used in general also stands bare: *Läkare vet…, Svenskar älskar…, Barn behöver…* — again just like English "Doctors know…". *Läkaren* in the line before is one particular doctor: Dian's.

**Livet är för kort** — here Swedish and English part ways. Abstract nouns used in general — life, death, love, nature, time, humanity — usually take the **definite** form in Swedish: *livet* (life), *döden* (death), *kärleken* (love), *naturen* (nature), *människan* (human beings). "Love is blind" is *Kärleken är blind*.

**Det här kaffet** / **detta kaffe** — the spoken and the written "this" side by side. Mattias switches to formal *detta* to sound grand, the way an English speaker might say "this fine brew". With *detta* the noun has no ending: *detta kaffe*, not *detta kaffet*.

**Båda sakerna** / **teet** — *båda* (both) takes the definite noun without *de*: *båda sakerna, båda barnen*. And *teet* (**TEH-et**) is "the tea": Dian means the particular tea she will drink this week, so it is definite. *Hålla sig till* = to stick to.

grammars.title: Talking in general: definite, indefinite or bare?
body: When you talk about something in general rather than a particular thing, English mostly uses no article. Swedish has three different solutions, depending on the kind of noun:

head: Type of noun
Swedish form
Example
English
rows: Do you have a car? I have a driver's license.

after: The "typical possession" rule covers things a person normally has one of: *Har du bil / cykel / jobb / körkort / pojkvän?* Adding *en* (*Har du en bil?*) is not wrong, but it sounds as if you are asking about one particular car.
A definite noun can also stand for a whole type, in a slightly literary style: *Svensken dricker mycket kaffe* = The (typical) Swede drinks a lot of coffee. *Människan* = humankind.

sections.title: The definiteness map for time expressions

blocks.text: Time expressions are where these rules matter most, because you use them every day. Here they are in one table — learn them row by row:

The pattern: **left column definite, right column indefinite**, and never a *den* in either. In the middle column, spoken Swedish uses *den här* + definite; in a formal letter you would write *denna vecka, denna månad, detta år*.

blocks.title: Three words that swallow den
items: **hela** — *hela dagen, hela tiden, hela familjen* (all day, all the time, the whole family)
**själva** — *själva poängen* (the whole point), *i själva verket* (in fact)
Compare *den långa dagen* (normal double definiteness) with *hela dagen* (no *den*).

head: Svenska
Pronunciation
English
rows: to stay home with a sick child

blocks.text: In Sweden, you **sjukanmäler dig** to your employer on the first morning you are ill, usually by phone or in an app. The first day is normally unpaid (*karensavdrag*); from the eighth day you need a doctor's certificate. Staying home with a fever is not just allowed but expected — Eva's "don't go to work" is standard advice.

Before you go to a *vårdcentral*, many Swedes call **1177**, the national health advice line, or use its website. A nurse assesses you and tells you whether to stay home, book an appointment or go to the emergency room. And *vabba* — staying home to care for a sick child, paid by the state — is so Swedish that the word does not translate into a single English verb.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 9
items: Combine possessives and *denna* with the participles from Unit 9. The adjective takes the definite ending, the noun does not: *min begagnade byrå*, *Dians målade stol*, *denna spännande film*.
Now add *hela*: without an adjective there is no *den* (*hela väggen*), but with an adjective *den* comes back (*hela den målade väggen*). Make three pairs like this of your own.
